note: Optional rule switches. Each one is off by default and can be turned on at the start screen, alone or together, with any balance package. All invention: rules, not history. Results for each are in docs/playtests/2026-11-22-switches.md. Jacob decides which, if any, become the default.

switches.name: Warnings are clues
switches.summary: Each plot warning comes from something the plotters really did: who they tried to win over, which grudge they played on, which faction or the guard took their money. A failed approach can reach your ears. Before, warnings were drawn from a pool of stock lines.

switches.name: Blows can miss
switches.summary: A strike that beats your defense by 1 or 2 only wounds you (you lose an action next season, and the leader flees the city). By 3 or 4 you live, but the leader seizes one of your offices and your house is plundered. Only a margin of 5 or more kills or exiles you.
switches.research: docs/game-research.md, proposal 3 (the smallest version of it)

switches.name: People escalate
switches.summary: A man asks for an office once. Refused, he waits a season and comes back with a demand, in public. Refuse the demand and he never asks for it again: he holds a grudge and acts. A man who was your rival before comes back a rank higher.

switches.name: A Pretender needs a coalition
switches.summary: A political rival rises to Pretender only if a second faction, not his own, is Angry or worse with you. While none is, his steps toward taking your place stall. Keep the other factions above Angry and no single man can vote you out.

switches.name: Chronicle as story
switches.summary: The chronicle follows people instead of listing events: each season is told by who it was about, with what led to it, and at the end each person's thread through the decade is gathered into a short life. No rules change.

switches.name: One feud record
switches.summary: Each person keeps one record with you that is never wiped. A pardon, a gift or an office pauses a feud; it does not end it, and a new wrong brings it back at its old rank. The same grievance can't start a feud twice. Enemies rise by surviving you: escaping your guards, living through their own failed blow, coming home from exile. Survive you twice and he is your Nemesis. Execute a man and his nearest kin takes up the feud. A political rival stays one until something decisive happens.

switches.name: Beaten armies can break
switches.summary: Island game only. An army beaten in battle with no food left, or beaten for the second time within a year, scatters instead of falling back. Before, a beaten army always fell back to a friendly town, so Carthage almost never lost an army.
switches.research: docs/handoff.md, "Broke or odd in the island"

switches.name: Your council argues
switches.summary: Four men sit at your table (five on the island, with a voice of the rich houses): the kinsman, the old friend, the purse and the sword. Before each action they say what they think, from their faction, their traits and what they know, and each season they tell you what worries them. A man who plots against you, wants your place or hates you gives counsel that serves himself: he shields his fellow plotters and points you at an innocent man. Watch the man he accused to catch him out. Proud men you overrule think less of you. You can seat whom you like.
switches.research: docs/game-research.md, proposal 4; the war council in Diodorus 14.8.5 (docs/research/council-and-secrets.md)

switches.name: Secrets and leverage
switches.summary: Leverage becomes named secrets: Philistus has married Leptines' daughter without telling you, Theodorus meets the exiles' riders by night. Watching a man shows what he is doing now; paying his servants tells what he did. A small secret is used up when you use it; a deadly one is a hold that rests and can be used again, even to make a man hand you his office. You have secrets too (the night alarm at Leontini, the rumors you planted, the men you blackmailed), and your rivals dig for them: they ask a price for silence, or tell the city. A hold on each side keeps both mouths shut. On the island you can send spies to a town's first man.

switches.name: A bought retreat disgraces the general
switches.summary: If you take Himilcon's secret bargain and let his Carthaginians sail home by night, Carthage treats it as a lost army: the general comes home in disgrace, the council's war party loses weight, and Himilcon may end as Diodorus says he did, starving himself in the temples.
switches.research: docs/research/island-events.md (A bargain by night; Diodorus 14.76.3 to 14.76.4)

switches.name: Rumors can lie
switches.summary: News from Carthage's council and from Libya is sometimes false: about one story in three. A false story changes nothing in Carthage, whatever you paid to act on it. Two seasons later, word comes whether it was true. Each rumor says so when it arrives.

switches.name: Lead the army yourself
switches.summary: Island game only. When you muster, you choose who leads: yourself or a named man, even without the generalship (passing over the general angers the citizens). If you go, you name a keeper of the citadel: plots at home gain 1 while you are away, and your keeper's loyalty adds to or takes from your defense. You fight 1 better in person. The levy arms the citizens, so a plot with a citizen in it gains 1 while the army is out. When the army comes home, a victory brings cheers: for you, the citizens' goodwill; for a man you sent, influence and a following of his own. Every price is shown before you muster.

switches.name: Dinners as the stage
switches.summary: A new action, Give a dinner. You choose who reclines on the couch beside yours, two to four other guests, and how strong the wine is mixed. The couch of honour adds to its holder's standing, and the man who held it before may take it badly. Each part of the evening can bring a moment from the guests themselves: two men become friends, two fall out, a plotter lets slip a name, a story about someone else comes out, or you say too much about a man who is not there. Some moments put a choice to you. Friends from your table plot together more easily; men who quarrelled there never do.

switches.name: Great works
switches.summary: Build power, not only hold it. Three great works can be begun: the Epipolae wall, the arms workshops and the great fleet. Each is built over seasons: you choose whose labour (peasants off the fields, hired men, craftsmen from your cities, from Italy and Greece, or lured from Carthage's lands) and who is set over it (yourself, at one action a season, a hired foreman, or a man whose people will be pleased). Every season it takes silver and food, unpaid men down tools, and the arms and the fleet anger Carthage. Done, they give walls, engines, armour, armed citizens and a fleet that brings grain. The old Build wall and the wall and workshop events give way to them.

switches.name: Grain and the sea
switches.summary: Island game only. Grain crosses the sea as convoys you can follow on the map. Grain you buy abroad, the fleet's winter grain and your allies' surplus sail to Syracuse and land a season later; you can send grain to your army if it stands on the coast. Each convoy is run by a contractor from one of the rich houses, who may skim it (it lands short, and he blames the sea), or at war, if the rich are angry, sell it to Carthage. You can audit his books, at the price of the rich families' goodwill. Winter storms sink or delay ships. At war, an enemy fleet catches a convoy on 5 or more, harder if your warships escort it. Carthage feeds its army and pays its mercenaries by sea too: catch its grain and its army goes hungry, catch its pay and its mercenaries desert.

switches.name: The purse runs dry
switches.summary: Striking coin and the levy on the rich families still pay once the rich are Rebellious, but less each time: every squeeze at the bottom takes 1 silver off the next, and their purses refill by 1 every four seasons. Without it, both pay in full forever once the rich can hate you no more. From the council of 2026-11-25. The idea, not the rate, has a source: under Dionysius "in five years men had contributed the whole of their substance" (Aristotle, Politics 1313b).

switches.name: A different first year
switches.summary: In the first four seasons every event that can happen is as likely as any other, and a draw with only one event on offer may bring nothing, so the year does not open the same way in most games (without it, A general's offer opens every island game). The brother of Demarchus' grudge, which is sourced, stays. From the council of 2026-11-25.

switches.name: Fallen, not finished
switches.summary: Island game only. Losing Syracuse is no longer the end. Deposed, driven out by a plot, or with the city taken by Carthage, you flee to a refuge (Aetna or a free town if it will have you, Rhegium across the strait, or the Campanians in Carthage's country) with a few loyal men and what silver you can carry, and someone else rules. Each season you plot your way back: letters to the factions, men sworn to you inside the walls, hired companies, arms for the citizens, patrons abroad, raids for plunder. The new ruler acts on a list of their own: courting the angry, purging your friends, offering you terms, and sending men to hunt you, with warnings before they strike. When the odds are good enough, you strike for the city. Win and you rule again; fail and you are thrown back, or die in the streets as Hermocrates did. Every price and every chance is shown before you commit. A kill or a decade in exile still ends the game.

switches.name: Begin fallen
switches.summary: Island game only, with Fallen, not finished. The game opens in exile: the revolt of 404 comes early and succeeds, the leader of the exiled cavalry rules Syracuse, and you are with the Campanians in Carthage's country. In the sources the revolt failed (Diodorus 14.8 to 14.9).

switches.name: Carthage's chronicle
switches.summary: Island game only. A second chronicle tells the same decade from Carthage's side, in Carthage's own terms: each year named for its two suffetes, the council's votes and who carried them, the general made king by law, the tribute, the levies in Libya, plague and defeat read as the anger of the gods. Every sentence comes from a line in the game's log and shows which one. No rules change.
switches.research: docs/research/carthage-chronicle.md (Diodorus 13.114, 14.47, 14.54.5, 14.76 to 14.77; Aristotle, Politics 1273a; the Marseille Tariff)

switches.name: Quarrels with terms
switches.summary: Two new actions. Swear a quarrel: stand up in the assembly and swear that within two or four seasons you will strip a man of his offices, drive him from the city, or shame him. A careful or friendly man gives way at once; anyone else refuses, takes a grudge, and his faction sours. Then Accuse him before the assembly, as often as you like before the day: the factions take sides as on a law (his own and any Angry with you stand with him, any Content with you stand with you), and a rich friend can pay the fines for the uproar. Make it good and the citizens warm to you, more if the oath was bold; let the day pass and the citizens sour, and he gains. Your rivals swear against you too, one at a time and in the open, to take an office or shame you, and you can buy them off, give them what they want, or face them down. Silence a man who has sworn against you and the city says so. At most two quarrels of yours open at once. From the council on Solium Infernum (2026-11-25). Public accusation is history: in 406 Dionysius "accused the generals of betraying their cause to the Carthaginians" and the people "immediately dismissed some of them from office" (Diodorus 13.91 to 13.92); the oath with a day set is invention.

switches.name: The contested board
switches.summary: The offices become seats people fight over. Each holder uses his seat every season, for you, for his own, or against you, and the seat card says what he did. A seventh seat, the captain of the guard: if he turns against you, the guard stops defending you. Seats change hands their own way: the assembly votes on its leader each spring, and on the generalship and the fleet while the city is free; the treasury and mint are granted; the captain and the citadel move only by force, betrayal or arrest. Holders dig in (New, Settled, Dug in, Unshakeable) and slip when away or beaten. Losing a seat is a crisis with three answers. A small cast climbs one ladder of standing (Notable, a power, a rival, a pretender), each step a scene; men with standing petition for the use of your seats; each rival makes one move of his own a year; and a man you hit three times answers. You can ask a holder for a favour, back a man at a vote, appoint the captain and give a city's command. Design: docs/council/2026-11-26-offices-rivals-events.md. How seats changed hands is history; the rules are invention.

switches.name: The guard dies only in battle
switches.summary: Jacob's rule after his second test. Only battle and storming kill your guard. Hunger, plague, desertion and the sea take the levy; if the levy is gone, the army breaks up and the guard marches home.

switches.name: Love holds a rival back
switches.summary: A political rival who is Devoted to you (opinion +3) climbs no higher than Contender while he stays Devoted. Let his love cool and he climbs again.

switches.name: Carthage holds what it takes
switches.summary: For eight seasons after Carthage takes a town, some of its men stay: an embassy or your army nearby is 2 harder there, and the wartime bonus for tribute towns is lost. Himilcon left Campanians "to guard the districts of Sicily" (Diodorus 14.8.5).

switches.name: Carthage spares Libya
switches.summary: Carthage stops raising Libyan levies once the Libyans are Angry, so its own levy no longer drives them into long revolts that keep its war away for years.

switches.name: The mint as an order
switches.summary: Striking coin at your own mint uses none of your three actions, once a season; but each season running costs the rich families one more step of mood. A friendly holder who strikes for you grows his following.

switches.name: Petitions come with an offer
switches.summary: A man who asks for the use of your seats offers something back: silver, men for the guard, or word of plots.

switches.name: The war as a story (war and geopolitics focus)
switches.summary: A war has a cause you can read, an aim for each side, a ledger of what happened, weariness on both sides and a peace with terms. Carthage announces its landings a season ahead, comes back after a revolt in Libya, raids your coast and courts your towns in a lull, and its council unites when you hold much of the island. War brings its own matters: what the war is for, an army that wants battle, a victor's welcome, envoys with terms.

switches.name: Towns that choose (war and geopolitics focus)
switches.summary: Each town's three leading houses lean to you, to Carthage or to the town alone, shown on the town's sheet. The houses tilt whether a town goes over, an ally whose houses cannot agree or that has no friend of yours sends no silver or men, a friend inside a town you besiege may open a gate, news of your defeat lets the other houses drive your friends out, and whoever takes a town puts a friend at its head. You court a house with gifts; Carthage courts them too.

switches.name: Moving and feeding (war and geopolitics focus)
switches.summary: An army feeds from the friendly towns within 4 days' march, and a big army needs more of them, so one giant army empties its own country. Its food shows as fed, short or starving, with the reason. Ravage burns a hostile town's crops for a year; Reinforce brings fresh men from a nearby town; an army kept in the field without a battle loses its allies one by one. On the map, drag your army's shield to a town to see the route and the towns that might go over.
